ai-generated-disclosure.written-by: An AI coding agent (Claude), under human direction and review.
ai-generated-disclosure.covers: Everything the fork adds: ipfilter/, docs/, RUNNER.xml, README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md.
ai-generated-disclosure.does-not-cover: Upstream's code, which is the application. No path upstream owns is modified by this fork, byte for byte, verified by git-object comparison against a recorded baseline rather than asserted.
ai-generated-disclosure.what-that-means: If you are evaluating the runner manager, none of the generated code is in your path - use upstream. If you are evaluating ipfilter/, it is a fail-closed access control, the category where plausible-looking wrong code is most expensive: a bug does not misbehave, it denies every caller, and that is indistinguishable from a quiet day. Read the tests; do not deploy it on our say-so.
ai-generated-disclosure.if-offered-upstream: Any upstream pull request carries the same disclosure. A maintainer deciding whether to spend review time is entitled to know how a patch was produced.

contribution-routing.rule:
Anything about webhooks, VM lifecycle, runner registration, GitHub App setup, Terraform under gcp/, the Dockerfile, or dependencies. https://github.com/Cyclenerd/google-cloud-github-runner/issues
A fix landed upstream reaches everyone running this tool, including us. A fix landed here reaches us and strands you on a fork.
See repo-map for the current set. These have nowhere upstream to go yet.

That is the situation the fork is arranged to prevent. Either the change belongs upstream, or it can be done by COMPOSITION from outside upstream's tree. The worked example is the IP allowlist: it needed to run before the application's own routing, and does that by wrapping the WSGI callable from a consumer's entrypoint - zero upstream lines changed. The technique generalises to anything else needing a place in the request path.
Cheaper to be redirected there than to maintain a divergence here.

evaluation-order.note: Stated plainly in CONTRIBUTING.md, because an unstated priority is a slower rejection.
evaluation-order.criterion: Does it benefit meshly.ai? This fork is maintained to run our CI.
Does it benefit the wider community?
evaluation-order.note: If (1) is no and (2) is yes, the right home is upstream or your own fork, and we will say so.

do-not-add.note: A PR that is mostly tooling config will be declined.

contribution-routing.do-not-add: No new linters, formatters, type checkers, taint analysers or language-specific scanners, and no CI jobs to run them. This is upstream's project with upstream's conventions; a fork that imposes its employer's toolchain on a volunteer codebase is a nuisance to everyone downstream. Style here is upstream's: flake8 --max-line-length=127, spaces, no trailing whitespace.

project.name: google-cloud-github-runner
project.author: Cyclenerd and contributors
project.tagline: Ephemeral just-in-time self-hosted GitHub Actions runners, native to Google Cloud.
project.shape: A Flask application on Cloud Run receives GitHub webhooks and creates a GCE VM per queued job from an instance template; the runner is ephemeral and the VM goes away after the job. No Kubernetes, no cluster, no long-lived runner pool. Developer-facing change is one line of workflow YAML.

softness.note: A gradient, not a badge. Keep these counts current -- a stale count is how 'we barely touch upstream' survives past the point of being true.
softness.upstream-doc-paths-diverged: 4 top-level, plus community health files under .github/ (never workflows)
softness.verdict: Soft on code, MEDIUM on documentation.
softness.what-keeps-it-soft: The divergence is confined to files that cannot change program behaviour, and that is enforced structurally rather than by intention: only top-level .md blobs can be declared, so no edit to the baseline can add app/ or requirements.txt to the exception set.

would-make-it-hard.trigger: Any modification to an upstream CODE path.
Carrying a patch series, or a merge of upstream changes we rewrote.
Our additions acquiring dependencies upstream does not have.
Any addition becoming load-bearing for the application rather than composed in.
Offering nothing upstream. A soft fork that never sends anything back is a slow hard fork.

issue-tracker.scope: the paths this fork ADDS; see repo-map for the current set

fork.issue-tracker: https://github.com/Meshly-Open-Source/google-cloud-github-runner/issues Anything about the runner manager itself goes upstream. Filing an upstream bug here makes it look tracked while nobody who can fix it is reading it.
fork.why: Somewhere to put code upstream does not have yet, without editing upstream's code to do it. Not customisation - there are no behaviour changes.
fork.what-it-buys: A version bump stays a fast-forward instead of a merge of code we did not write. Specifically it rules out a patch that applies WITH FUZZ, which succeeds, now means something different, fails nothing, and is read by nobody.
fork.auditability: You can audit this fork without reading a diff: we changed nothing and added directories.
fork.default-branch: main (upstream's is master - the two differ, which is a trap for anything fetching by branch name)

fork-invariants.invariant:
Every path upstream owns is byte-identical here, EXCEPT an explicitly baselined set of top-level .md files, each pinned by its exact blob hash. Everything the fork adds is a new top-level path.
State the exception when you state the invariant. "Nothing differs" is a stronger claim than what is enforced, and a pass read as the stronger claim is worse than no check.
Checked by comparing git object ids against a recorded baseline of upstream's tree. That is a Merkle comparison: `app` matching means every file beneath it matches, recursively, byte for byte.

Only top-level .md BLOBS can be declared as divergences. A nested path or a non-.md path cannot be declared no matter how the baseline is edited, so app/, requirements.txt, Dockerfile and .github/ can never become exceptions.
This is the restriction that actually protects the application. An exclusion list would fail open on the next vendor path somebody wanted to touch; a structural predicate plus per-path hash pinning does not.
A declared divergence is pinned to an exact blob hash, so editing it again fails the check until it is deliberately re-baselined. Declaring a file is not a standing permission to change it.

No patches, no cherry-picks, no merge commits carrying upstream changes we rewrote. Upstream is tracked by commit. A patch series is worse than a fork because the bad outcome is a patch applying with fuzz.
requirements.txt is upstream's and unmodified. ipfilter/ is stdlib-only, so an addition of ours can never silently widen an upstream pin.
ipfilter/ is not imported by, referenced by, or enabled in the application. That is why app/ does not need to move. Enabling it is a composition step in a consumer's own deployment entrypoint.

application-facts.note: Facts an agent needs to compose with the app. Upstream's README is authoritative for behaviour.

composition-surface.note: Why wrapping works without editing anything

fact.what: create_app() is a FACTORY: it builds the Flask object inside the function and returns it. There is no module-level Flask singleton, so importing upstream does not commit a consumer to upstream's wiring.
Import is side-effect-free in the ways that matter: config reads use os.environ.get, never the raising subscript form, so an import cannot die on missing configuration.

Zero after_request and zero errorhandler hooks under app/. The only hook is a before_request in app/routes/setup.py, blueprint-scoped to /setup/*. Nothing upstream sits between a WSGI wrapper and a request.
The container runs `gunicorn run:app`, so upstream's entrypoint is merely 'a module exposing an app attribute'. A consumer provides its own module of the same shape.

routes.note: The complete route set, enumerated from app/. Useful as the coverage target for an ipfilter policy table - a table missing any of these fails startup.

route.auth: HMAC X-Hub-Signature-256, verified by an INLINE CALL inside the handler (app/utils/security.py), not a decorator and not a before_request

does-not-exist.note: There is no preemption-notice route at the pinned commit. A Spot-preempted VM posting to one gets a 404, silently. Relevant upstream work exists in flight; check before building it here.

application-facts.ordering-consequence: The /webhook HMAC check is an inline call inside the handler. A WSGI wrapper therefore runs BEFORE it. That ordering is correct for defence in depth, and it is also the hazard: a bug in the outer layer blocks a legitimate caller before HMAC can validate them, making the outer layer strictly more load-bearing than the control it backstops. Deploy log_only first, with a "no webhooks accepted recently" alarm in place BEFORE enforcing.

environment-variables.note: Names read from app/. See upstream's README for semantics.

fact.what: Python 3.14-alpine base, two-stage build with a wheelhouse so the production stage needs no compiler. Runs as a non-root appuser.

GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS bakes --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT with $PORT EXPANDED AT BUILD TIME to 8080. It looks like a runtime reference and is not: changing the Cloud Run port alone leaves gunicorn bound to 8080 and the container failing its startup probe. Change both or neither.
1 worker, 8 threads, timeout 0. A filter must therefore be thread-safe and hold no per-request state; ipfilter holds none.
Scale-to-zero is normal, so cold-start cost and image-pull failures surface at unrelated times rather than at deploy.

addition.name: ipfilter/
addition.tagline: An IP allowlist you can be wrong about safely.
addition.specification: ipfilter/tests/ - 149 tests. The prose is not authoritative; these are.
addition.proof-command-note: Pass the directory EXPLICITLY. testpaths resolves against pytest's inferred rootdir, which differs between a bare run and one with arguments; a bare run picks up the project's own Flask-dependent suite and fails collection. A proof command that works only when invoked one particular way is not a proof command.
addition.vendor-neutral-by-design: Named for what it does rather than for us, imports no web framework, and takes no dependency on this application, so an upstream offer is "add exactly this directory" - no renames, no imports to unpick.

key-properties.property: Zero CIDRs in the package, asserted by a test walking every module. A library default range set would turn one consumer's allowlist into a silent default for every future consumer. The consumer supplies named sets; a policy naming an unsupplied set is UNEVALUABLE, which under fail-closed denies.

allow / deny / UNEVALUABLE. "Not on the list" and "we have no list" have opposite implications and different owners; a single denied counter conflates them, and the conflation is how a stopped range refresher gets investigated as an attack. The collapse to a block happens at the enforcement edge as a configured fail mode, reason preserved.

v4 and v6 get separate compiled tables and parse paths. inet_pton(AF_INET6, "1.2.3.4") RAISES, so a single v6-shaped parse path puts every IPv4 caller in an except branch and, under fail-closed, denies them all silently.

No default anywhere. A default is correct for exactly one proxy topology and silently wrong for the rest; wrong here denies 100% of callers. An out-of-range index reports chain-shorter-than-index rather than falling back, because a fallback hides exactly that. MEASURE it from a recorded chain before enforcing.

An uncovered route is a STARTUP failure, asserted against the route set read from the running application rather than a grep (a grep cannot see a conditionally registered blueprint or a route built in a loop). A route that takes no address check is declared as such and must carry a written justification. A table that lets unknown routes through is an inclusion list, and it fails open on the route added next week by someone who never read it.

Every decision emits one JSON line carrying the full chain, the index used, the derived address, the peer, the policy and a discriminated reason. A fail-closed filter fails QUIETLY - no error, no exception, no failed request - so the record is the only evidence the control works and the only way a wrong index is diagnosable. json.dumps also means an attacker-supplied header cannot forge a second log line.

All decisions live in enforcement.py; the WSGI and ASGI adapters only translate transport. A 14-case parity test asserts identical verdicts, because two adapters that each implement the decision will drift and the drift surfaces on whichever stack gets less traffic.

build-and-deploy.note: Only relevant if you build your own image. If you do not have that concern, use upstream's Cloud Build template - less work, and maintained.
build-and-deploy.why-self-build: One reason, and it is not customisation: the tree you review and the artifact you run should be the same thing. A build invoked from outside your repository is a build nobody reviews - the same defect shape as a deploy script generated at deploy time.
build-and-deploy.trap: `gcloud builds submit` uploads a SOURCE TARBALL. Inside the build there is no .git, no commit, no submodule state. Any check needing git objects must run in the wrapper that invokes the submit, not in the build config - and that wrapper must be the documented entry point, or the check is one typed command away from being skipped.

An uninitialised submodule is an EMPTY DIRECTORY and COPY of one succeeds. The build then produces an image missing the code it was meant to contain, with no error anywhere. Same shape as a guard that passes having checked nothing.

Upstream copies only requirements.txt before the expensive `pip wheel` layer, so a code edit does not recompile every wheel. Copy source in before that RUN - which looks tidier - and every one-line change pays the full compile. Add your own code AFTER upstream's, since upstream changes rarely and yours changes often.

An unpullable --cache-from source is not an error. The build proceeds without a cache and is simply slower, indistinguishable from a cache miss. A build quietly 4x slower forever is a cost nobody notices because nothing failed.

A digest-pinned image is UNTAGGED from Artifact Registry's point of view, so a policy deleting untagged images deletes what production runs. Nothing fails until the next cold start, at an unrelated time, with no deploy having happened.

Apache-2.0 permits redistributing a derivative image provided the licence travels with it. Ensure LICENSE lands inside the image beside the code it covers, and that no .dockerignore rule excludes it. It is a one-line omission that turns permitted redistribution into unlicensed, silently.

The runtime service account needs artifactregistry.reader on the repository, which is easy to miss when build and runtime are different identities. Symptom: the deploy succeeds and the revision never becomes healthy, with the pull failure in the revision's logs rather than the deploy output.

agent-empathy.note: Observed failure modes in THIS repo. Read before editing.

struggle.problem: Editing an upstream file because it is the shortest path

agent-empathy.struggle: It is always the shortest path, and it is the one thing the fork exists to prevent. Ask whether the change can be made by composition from outside upstream's tree. For a request-path concern the answer is usually yes: create_app() is a factory and there are no app-level request hooks, so wrapping the WSGI callable gets you in front of everything.

struggle.problem: Writing a fork-specific feature into app/ 'for now'

agent-empathy.struggle: There is no "for now". The divergence check fails, and if it is softened to let the change through, the next upstream bump becomes a merge.

struggle.problem: Adding a linter, formatter or CI job

agent-empathy.struggle: Deliberately absent. This is upstream's project with upstream's conventions; style is flake8 --max-line-length=127. See the contribution-routing / do-not-add sections.
Bare pytest picks up upstream's suite, which needs Flask installed and fails collection. That is an environment failure, not a fork failure. Use the explicit proof command for ipfilter.

struggle.problem: Treating a green test run as proof the tests work

agent-empathy.struggle: They are a claim until a mutation turns them red. During this package's own development a sed-based mutation silently failed to apply and reported 149 passed - which read exactly like a surviving mutant. Assert the mutation LANDED before believing the result.

struggle.problem: Reading an exit code through a pipe

agent-empathy.struggle: `cmd | tail; echo $?` reports tail's status, not cmd's. It produced wrong claims in this session. Redirect to a file, or capture the status directly.

struggle.problem: Assuming the fork's default branch matches upstream's

agent-empathy.struggle: This fork is `main`; upstream is `master`. Anything fetching by branch name needs the right one for each, and the pinned commit resolves on both.

struggle.problem: Building /runner/preempted here because a VM 404s on it

agent-empathy.struggle: Check upstream's open work first. A preemption notice is the kind of thing that belongs upstream, and duplicating in-flight upstream work is how a fork acquires a divergence it then has to maintain.

struggle.problem: Reading a byte-identity pass as 'nothing differs'

agent-empathy.struggle: Three top-level .md files are declared divergences, each pinned by hash. The guarantee is narrower than the headline; state the exception when you state the invariant.
